The air in an empty room weighs roughly 1.2 kilograms per cubic meter, but this calculation assumes standard atmospheric pressure and takes no account of who has lived there. 

Julian kept this number written on an index card taped above his workbench, beneath three rusted brass calipers and a row of glass jars filled with dry pigments: bone black, raw umber, burnt sienna, and a chalky, pale blue he called *morning water*. Julian was a surveyor, though not of roads or municipal boundaries. People came to him when they had lost a place that never had a deed.

He worked on the second floor of a narrow brick building wedged between a bakery and an upholstery shop. Below, the baker pulled loaves from the brick oven at four in the morning, filling the floorboards with the smell of scorched crust and yeast; to his left, the upholsterer spent his afternoons rhythmically driving tacks into horsehair cushions. Between the bread and the hammers, Julian measured things that had ceased to exist.

A woman climbed the stairs on a Tuesday in November, when the rain had turned the color of greasy tin. Her name was Clara. She did not take off her coat—a dark wool thing frayed at the cuffs—and she carried a brass key on a string.

"The building was torn down six years ago," she said, sitting on the stool across from his desk without being invited. "They built a parking garage with three levels and an automated ticket arm. But my mother lived on the third floor for forty-two years. She had a balcony that faced west. In June, the light would hit the linoleum and make it look like honey."

"Do you have photographs?" Julian asked.

"Two," she said. "One of my brother on his sixth birthday, but the flash failed, so you can only see his white collar and the red cherry on the cake. And one of a cat sleeping on a radiator."

"The radiator is very useful," Julian told her gently. "Radiators have standard dimensions. If we know the manufacturer, we know the height, which gives us the window sill, which gives us the wall."

He reached for a fresh sheet of vellum, thick and slightly waxy, and clipped it to the drafting board. He dipped a steel nib into sepia ink.

"Tell me about the sound of the stairs," he said.

This was always where he began. Footsteps established scale. A person does not walk up thirteen steps the same way she walks up fourteen. The eighth riser in an old house almost always dips three millimeters to the center, because people favor their right foot when carrying groceries.

Clara closed her eyes. Her fingers, red from the cold, worked the brass key around its twine loop. "There were twenty-six steps from the vestibule to her landing. A turn to the left after twelve. The wood was yellow pine, covered in brown rubber treads that had worn down so the nails poked through near the edge. You had to step wide."

"Wide," Julian repeated, making a tiny, precise mark with a 4H pencil. "And the door?"

"Green. Three coats over dark varnish. If you pushed it, it stuck at the bottom against the saddle until you lifted the brass handle slightly."

"A settling hinge," Julian murmured. "Four millimeters of drop."

They worked for three hours while the November afternoon surrendered entirely to the rain. Clara spoke not in descriptions of style, but of resistances: the drawer that refused to open when the humidity was high; the draft that found the space between the baseboard and the floorboards near the hall closet, cold enough to freeze an onion left in a basket; the smell of chicory and gas that lingered near the stove; the square of floral wallpaper behind the pantry door where the previous tenant had pasted over a water stain.

Julian drew. His hand did not waver. He laid down construction lines so light they looked like spider silk caught in a window sash. He laid down floor joists that no one had seen since 1911. He calculated the pitch of the ceiling from the shadow behind the sleeping cat on the radiator.

"Here," he said, turning the board toward her.

It was not a picture; it was an orthographic projection. It showed the third-floor apartment as if viewed from above by an impossible eye that could see through plaster, through decades, through the three levels of reinforced concrete that now occupied that coordinates of space. The rooms were delineated with fine, double-inked lines, their thresholds notched with tiny arcs showing the swing of doors that had long since burned in a municipal incinerator.

Clara leaned over the vellum. She did not touch it—she knew ink took time to dry in damp weather—but she hovered her palm an inch above the small rectangle marked *Pantry*.

"The shelves were deeper," she said softly.

Julian picked up his horn scraper. With surgical delicacy, he lifted two hairs’ width of dried ink from the page, blew away the fine black dust, and ruled the line three millimeters back toward the chimney breast.

"Like that?"

"Yes," she whispered. "Like that. My father kept his tobacco tin on the top shelf, behind the vinegar bottles, where he thought we couldn't reach it."

She stayed for another twenty minutes, watching the lines settle into the grain of the paper. She did not cry. In Julian’s experience, people rarely cried over maps. Maps appealed to the part of the brain that organizes survival; they implied that return was possible, even if one only returned with the finger tracing a path through ink.

When she left, she insisted on leaving the brass key on his blotter.

"It doesn't turn anything now," she said. "It just makes holes in my pockets."

Julian sat alone under the cone of his green-shaded lamp after her footsteps had faded down the twenty-two stairs of his own building—steps he had measured once, thirty years ago, and never thought about since. 

Outside, the streetlights came on, halos of amber grease against the wet black pavement. A truck rumbled past, rattling the pane in its frame. Julian touched the surface of the vellum. It was cool.

He thought of all the rooms hovering in the dark above the cities of the world: second floors that had been replaced by empty air, bedrooms where children had had measles, kitchens where tea had boiled over onto iron grates, all occupying elevations that now belonged only to pigeons, telephone cables, and the cold, unmetered rain. 

He took the brass key and dropped it into a drawer full of other keys—square-shanked, iron, nickel-plated, notched—each one an orphan of an address that had dissolved. Then he blew out the lamp, leaving the drawing to cure in the dark, where it occupied no space at all.
